blocks.md:
The shipped [retool generate function](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/79aa41a884ab0bf65222c94418f6357d3c31192b/examples/retool/generate_with_retool.py) adds the parts a real loop needs: it clamps each turn's `max_new_tokens` to the remaining context budget, trims tool output that would overflow and marks the sample `TRUNCATED`, and aborts the sample if SGLang returns no log probs. Its reward function scores the final boxed answer with the DAPO math checker and, when the answer is wrong, gives a slightly less negative score to trajectories that called the tool more.

Note the payload: retool sends `input_ids`, so turn 1 conditions on the exact ids sampled in turn 0. The search-r1 example sends text instead and lets the server re-tokenize, which works but can drift from the ids it trained on (the RL infrastructure course, lesson 9, explains token-in, token-out).

If the agent already exists in a framework, slime's [agent roadmap](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/docs/en/get_started/agent.md) recommends adapters instead of rewriting it. `slime.agent.adapters.AnthropicAdapter` (Messages API, as used by Claude Code style agents) and `OpenAIAdapter` (Chat Completions and Responses APIs) expose an HTTP app your agent client talks to: messages in, sampled tokens out. They render the chat template, call SGLang with `input_ids` and `return_logprob=True`, and `finish_session` returns trainable segments without re-tokenizing. A stable `session_id` is sent as a routing key so one session's turns hit the same worker and reuse its prefix cache.

A custom generate function may also return a **list** of samples, for example when a subagent and the main agent should both be trained, or when context compaction splits a trajectory. The contract is that siblings share the same `rollout_id`, so GRPO counts them as one rollout. If the trajectory has a single outcome reward, every segment gets that same reward; the docs warn that dividing it by the segment count would underweight trajectories split into more segments.

Put per-sample agent logic in a custom generate function and scoring in a custom reward function. You keep slime's batching, dynamic sampling, abort and partial-rollout machinery for free, and your code works unchanged under fully async rollout.

blocks.question: Your agent calls a code interpreter between model turns and appends the interpreter output to the response. Training loss starts rewarding the model for "predicting" interpreter output. What is the bug?
options: The reward function should return a list
You need --rollout-function-path instead of a custom generate function
The router should be bypassed for tool calls
Tool output tokens were appended with trainable=True instead of trainable=False, so they are in the loss mask
blocks.explain: Only model-generated tokens should carry loss. The search-r1 example appends observation tokens with `trainable=False` (loss mask 0). Swapping hook types does not fix a wrong mask.

blocks.question: With --rollout-batch-size 3, --over-sampling-batch-size 6 and the zero-std filter, all 6 groups finish and only 2 have non-zero reward std. What does the default loop do?
options: Trains on the 2 groups it has
Pads the batch with dropped groups
Fetches another 6 groups from the Data Buffer, since kept plus in-flight groups fell below the target of 3
Raises an error immediately
blocks.explain: Each dropped group lowers the in-flight count; when it falls below the target, the loop submits another --over-sampling-batch-size groups. It returns only when it has exactly rollout_batch_size kept groups.

lessons.title: The trainer side: from scored samples to a policy-gradient step

blocks.md:
Lesson 1's diagram had a box that said the Megatron actor "recomputes log probs, computes advantages and the loss". This lesson opens it, using the group from lesson 5: one prompt, four responses with rewards 1, 0, 1, 1.

Where those samples start: `--prompt-data` is a JSONL or Parquet file, and each record holds a prompt under `--input-key` (default `input`) and a label under `--label-key`. With `--apply-chat-template` the prompt is an OpenAI-style message list that the tokenizer's chat template renders into text; `--metadata-key` carries extra fields to custom functions. The example script reads `prompt` and `label` from dapo-math-17k, and the label is what the reward function compares answers against.

What reaches the trainer is not text. [BatchBuilder.convert](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/79aa41a884ab0bf65222c94418f6357d3c31192b/slime/data/batch_builder.py) turns each finished Sample into training fields: `tokens` (prompt plus response ids), `response_lengths`, `loss_masks` (1 for model tokens, 0 for tool or masked tokens), `rewards`, `raw_reward`, `rollout_ids`, and `rollout_log_probs` when the engine returned them. Megatron later adds three per-token arrays of its own: reference log probs, old log probs and, during the step, the trainable policy's log probs.

blocks.title: Where each piece of the update is computed

nodes.label:
split over DP ranks
+ dynamic batches

scenes.caption: Rewards are group-normalized before Megatron sees them, in the rollout manager's BatchBuilder. The batch is then split across data-parallel ranks and packed into micro-batches by token budget.
If a KL term is configured, the reference weights are swapped into the same Megatron model for one no-gradient forward pass that records ref_log_probs.
The actor weights come back and another no-gradient pass records the old log probs p0. slime skips this pass when the training forward would produce the same numbers anyway.
Advantages are computed for every response token from the normalized rewards (and, for some estimators, KL or a critic).
Only now does the gradient pass run: it computes p_theta, the clipped policy loss and optional entropy and KL terms, then one optimizer step per global batch.

blocks.md: **Step 1, rewards.** For the estimators `grpo`, `gspo`, `cispo` and `reinforce_plus_plus_baseline`, BatchBuilder subtracts each prompt group's mean reward; for the first three it also divides by the group's standard deviation plus 1e-6. `--disable-grpo-std-normalization` drops the division (the flag's help cites Dr. GRPO, [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783)), and `--disable-rewards-normalization` drops both. The code uses PyTorch's default `std()`, the sample standard deviation that divides by $G-1$, not by $G$.

blocks.caption: For rewards 1, 0, 1, 1: mean 0.75, centered 0.25, -0.75, 0.25, 0.25, s = 0.5, so A = 0.5, -1.5, 0.5, 0.5. With the population convention (divide by G), used in the GRPO and RLVR course, s would be 0.433. The experiment guide quotes the same convention: sqrt(2/7) for four 1s and four 0s.

blocks.md:
**Step 2, reference and old log probs.** The reference model is loaded from `--ref-load` only when `--use-kl-loss` is set or `--kl-coef` is non-zero. It is not a second model on the GPU: the actor keeps a pinned CPU copy of every parameter per tag ("actor", "ref") and copies the reference tensors into the live model for one forward pass, then copies the actor back. `--ref-update-interval N` refreshes the reference from the actor every N rollouts.

The old log probs p0 are recomputed by the actor, not taken from SGLang. slime skips that extra forward when there is one training step per rollout and nothing else needs p0 separately (among the conditions: no reward-side KL, no mismatch metrics, no critic, not GSPO): the training forward then sees the same weights, so its detached values are p0. The catch: first-step `ppo_kl` is then 0 by construction, so it can only expose non-deterministic kernels in runs where the separate pass does run. `--use-rollout-logprobs` skips it too, by using SGLang's numbers as the old policy (lesson 8).

**Step 3, advantages.** For `grpo`, `gspo` and `cispo` every token of a response gets the response's normalized reward. Two KL knobs are easy to confuse. `--kl-coef` shapes the reward with a per-token KL penalty, which only the `ppo` and REINFORCE++ estimators use: GRPO's returns ignore it. GRPO's KL belongs in the loss through `--use-kl-loss --kl-loss-coef`, as in DeepSeekMath, and slime refuses to set both coefficients; `--kl-loss-type low_var_kl` is the $k_3$ estimator from the GRPO course. `--normalize-advantages` whitens advantages over the whole data-parallel group.

**Step 4, the loss.** `policy_loss_function` in [loss.py](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/79aa41a884ab0bf65222c94418f6357d3c31192b/slime/backends/megatron_utils/loss.py) computes `ppo_kl = old - new` per token and the PPO clipped surrogate with `--eps-clip` (default 0.2) below and `--eps-clip-high` above (defaults to the same value; set it higher for DAPO's clip-higher). Why the clip keeps the larger loss is worked through in the GRPO and RLVR course, lesson 4. Here are slime's lines on one response.

blocks.title: slime's policy loss on one response (A = +0.5, eps 0.2)
blocks.code:
ppo_kl = old_log_probs - log_probs        # per token
ratio = (-ppo_kl).exp()
pg1 = -ratio * advantages
pg2 = -ratio.clamp(1 - eps_clip, 1 + eps_clip_high) * advantages
pg_loss = torch.maximum(pg1, pg2)
clipfrac = (pg2 > pg1).float()
if args.use_tis:
    pg_loss = pg_loss * tis_weights          # lesson 8
pg_loss = reducer(pg_loss)                  # per sample or per token
loss = pg_loss - args.entropy_coef * reducer(entropy)
if args.use_kl_loss:
    loss = loss + args.kl_loss_coef * reducer(kl(log_probs, ref_log_probs))

scenes.caption: A correct response (advantage +0.5) with 3 tokens. p0 log probs -1.20, -0.90, -2.00; after some updates the policy gives -1.10, -0.50, -2.40.
Unclipped terms are -ratio x A. The clipped ratios are 1.105, 1.2 and 0.8, so the clipped terms are -0.553, -0.600 and -0.400.
Taking the larger (pessimistic) loss: token 2 already rose past 1.2, so it is capped; token 3 moved the wrong way and keeps its full correction. One of three tokens is counted as clipped.
Optional behavior correction multiplies each token's loss by a detached weight; it is off in this example.
The reducer turns token losses into one number. Then entropy and KL terms are added; with both coefficients 0 the loss is just the policy term.
At the first step of a rollout the weights still equal those that produced p0, so ppo_kl is 0, every ratio is 1, nothing clips, and each token's loss is exactly -A = -0.5.

blocks.md: The reducer is where two otherwise identical runs differ. By default slime averages each sample's tokens and then averages samples: the per-sample denominator is the loss-mask total of that sample's rollout (the `rollout_mask_sums` field, so segments a custom generate function returned under one `rollout_id` share one denominator), and Megatron's scaling turns the sum over samples into a mean. `--calculate-per-token-loss` instead sums every token's loss and divides by the total token count.

blocks.caption: N responses, T_i loss-masked tokens in response i, token loss l. The worked example: response A above (3 tokens, sum -1.488) and a wrong response B with advantage -1.5 and 9 tokens at ratio 1 (loss 1.5 each). Per sample: (-0.496 + 1.5) / 2 = 0.502. Per token: (-1.488 + 13.5) / 12 = 1.001.

blocks.title: How much each token counts: per-sample vs per-token loss

scenes.caption: Default per-sample mean: each response weighs 1/2, split over its own tokens. A short response's tokens count 1/6 each, a long one's 1/18.
--calculate-per-token-loss: every token weighs 1/12, so the 9-token response carries three quarters of the update. Long wrong answers are penalized harder than under the default.

blocks.md:
The other `--advantage-estimator` values, one line each:

- `gspo` ([GSPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071)): one ratio per sequence, the exponential of the mean token log ratio, shared by all its tokens.
- `cispo` (MiniMax-M1): clips the ratio under stop-gradient and multiplies it into the log probability, so clipped tokens still pass gradient.
- `reinforce_plus_plus` ([REINFORCE++](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.03262)): no critic; the reward sits on the last token, the KL penalty on every token, and returns are discounted with `--gamma`.
- `reinforce_plus_plus_baseline`: the group-mean-centered reward minus the per-token KL penalty.
- `ppo`: a critic with GAE (`--gamma`, `--lambd`); actor and critic share the training GPUs and must use identical parallel topology, and `--num-critic-only-steps` warms the critic up first.

Separately, `--pg-loss-type reinforce` replaces the clipped surrogate with $-A \log p_\theta$: no ratio, no clip, `pg_clipfrac` always 0. Score centering requires it and lesson 9's script uses it; at ratio 1 its gradient equals PPO's.

In slime the update is split across two places: reward normalization happens in the rollout manager, everything else on the Megatron actor in the order reference log probs, old log probs, advantages, loss. Most algorithm changes are flags on that path (estimator, normalization, clip bounds, KL placement, reducer); `--custom-advantage-function-path` and `--loss-type custom_loss` replace a stage outright.

blocks.question: slime's CI asserts that `ppo_kl` at the first training step of every rollout is below 1e-8. Why should it be zero there?
options: Before the first optimizer step of a rollout the trainable weights are the ones that produced p0, so new and old log probs come from the same weights and inputs
Because the reference model is reloaded at every rollout
Because GRPO advantages sum to zero within a group
Because the PPO clip forces the ratio to 1 at the first step
blocks.explain: ppo_kl is old minus new log probs per token. At the first step nothing has been updated since p0 was computed, so only non-deterministic kernels or a bug can make it non-zero (and only when p0 came from a separate pass; otherwise it is 0 by construction). The reference model and advantages do not enter ppo_kl, and the clip limits the loss, not the ratio.

blocks.question: A run uses `--advantage-estimator grpo --kl-coef 0.05`, hoping to keep the policy near the reference. The reference model loads and slime computes a per-token KL, yet training behaves exactly like a run without KL. Why?
options: The KL is computed against the wrong checkpoint
--kl-coef is ignored unless --colocate is set
The coefficient is too small to matter
--kl-coef only shapes rewards for ppo and REINFORCE++; GRPO's advantages ignore it. Use --use-kl-loss --kl-loss-coef instead
blocks.explain: compute_advantages_and_returns computes the KL whenever kl_coef is non-zero, but get_grpo_returns copies only the reward to every token. GRPO's KL term goes into the loss, and slime asserts that kl_coef and kl_loss_coef are not both set.

lessons.title: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness

blocks.md:
A synchronous round waits for its slowest sample. For agentic tasks, where one trajectory may run many tool calls in a sandbox, that tail can dominate. slime's answer does **not** add a second training loop: train.py stays the only entrypoint, and fully async behavior lives in a different rollout function:

`--rollout-function-path slime.rollout.fully_async_rollout.generate_rollout_fully_async`

On first call it starts an `AsyncRolloutWorker`: a background thread with its own asyncio loop that keeps generating groups across rollout boundaries. Each `generate_rollout` call just drains the ready queue until it has `--rollout-batch-size` groups; the surplus stays queued for the next call ("the queue stays warm").

blocks.caption: From slime's rl-systems guide. A synchronous round costs rollout plus training plus weight update. Overlapped, it costs at least the longer of rollout and training, plus the update. t_R is rollout plus reward time, t_T training, t_W weight update.

blocks.title: Round time: synchronous vs ideal overlap

scenes.caption: Lesson 2's illustrative round: t_R = 300 s, t_T = 120 s, t_W = 48 s. Serial: 468 s. Perfect overlap: max(300, 120) + 48 = 348 s, at most 1.345x faster.

When training is as long as rollout (t_T = 300 s at t_R = 300 s), overlap helps most: 648 s serial versus 348 s, about 1.86x. The two marked points still show the t_T = 120 s case from the first scene.
Weight sync is paid in both curves. With t_W = 0 the bound becomes max(t_R, t_T); a slow sync shrinks the gain. These are optimistic lower bounds, not predictions.

blocks.md: How much work is in flight? The worker's budget is `--sglang-server-concurrency` (default 512) times the number of engines, divided by `n_samples_per_prompt` to get prompt-group slots. With 8 rollout GPUs in 2-GPU engines (4 engines) and n = 8, that is 512 x 4 / 8 = 256 groups generating at once. `--fully-async-group-prefetch-factor` can enlarge the group pool so slow group members do not leave sample slots idle.

That worker lives inside the rollout manager process. For larger agentic jobs the [rollout-scheduling guide](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/docs/en/advanced/rollout-scheduling.md) describes a second mode with the same rollout function path: select straw transport and it uses `DistributedRollout`, one CPU generation actor on every eligible Ray node, all sending requests to the same SGLang engines. They are producers, not model replicas. The group-slot budget $K = \lfloor CE/G \rfloor$ (concurrency $C$, engines $E$, samples per prompt $G$) is split across the $W$ workers, and each needs at least one group, so $CE \ge WG$: in the example above, at most 256 producer nodes.

blocks.title: Distributed fully async rollout with straw

scenes.caption: Prompt groups and partial rollouts are tasks in a queue on shared storage. Each producer takes tasks under a renewable lease, so work held by a lost producer becomes available again when its lease expires.
Producers drive generation, tools and rewards against the shared SGLang engines; their concurrency comes out of the K group slots.
Finished groups and their tensors (tokens, log probs, R3 routes) are written to storage in packed files, about 1 GiB each by default, instead of travelling through Ray's object store.

The collector builds a batch from completed groups first, then partial ones, then fresh prompts, older weight versions first. Fast producers can fill a batch without waiting for slow ones. Stale samples are ordered, not dropped.

blocks.md: straw is enabled with `--rollout-data-transport straw --rollout-data-dir /shared/.../rollout_data --rollout-queue-run-id my-run`. Multi-node runs also need `--rollout-storage-profile juicefs` and `--rollout-storage-declaration` (a JSON file describing the mount): JuiceFS, mounted at the same path on every node, is the supported shared filesystem, and the default profile, `local`, is for development. Because tasks, partial and ready groups, training batches and packed tensors are all on disk, two things become possible: producers can be lost and replaced through leases, and a failed trainer can replay the batches after its last checkpoint (lesson 10). It does not restore GPU KV cache or guarantee identical future random generations.

blocks.title: Fully async: generation keeps running across steps

scenes.caption: Same illustrative times on separate pools. A background worker keeps a fixed pool of in-flight generations; groups that finish go to a ready queue.
Training on batch 1 starts as soon as enough groups are ready, while generation for the next batch continues on the same weights v1.

Admission pauses for the sync. With --flush-cache-interval 0 unfinished requests pause in place and continue on v2; the default 1 aborts them and requeues their groups. Samples begun under v1 and finished under v2 are stale by one version.

blocks.md: The cost of overlap is **staleness**. If a sample was generated with weight version $v_s$ and trained at version $v_t$, its age is $d = v_t - v_s$. slime logs `staleness/mean` and `staleness/max`. The rl-systems guide splits the log-prob gap into two parts:

blocks.tex: \log p_{v_t}(a\mid h)-\log q_{v_s}(a\mid h)=\underbrace{\log p_{v_t}-\log p_{v_s}}_{\text{parameter staleness}}+\underbrace{\log p_{v_s}-\log q_{v_s}}_{\text{same-version engine mismatch}}
blocks.caption: In words: the trainer-versus-rollout gap for token a after history h is how far the weights moved since v_s plus how far the engine differs from the trainer at v_s. p is the trainer, q the engine. Deterministic kernels shrink only the second.

blocks.md: Two related details from the source. Groups that contain an aborted sample are pushed back to the Data Buffer instead of being sent to training. And `--flush-cache-interval` controls the KV cache at each sync: the default 1 aborts in-flight requests and flushes every sync; 0 or less always pauses in place and keeps unfinished sequences across the update (the PipelineRL style, after a ServiceNow system that updates weights in the middle of generation); and N greater than 1 does the same except for a full flush every N syncs. The argument help says values other than 1 select fully async rollout by default and require separate GPUs.

Fully async needs separate rollout and training GPUs to overlap anything, and its README lists no evaluation mode (it would conflict with the continuously running model), so evaluate with a separate path or job. Importance-sampling corrections such as TIS (lesson 8) help with mismatch, but the docs say they do not justify an unlimited stale queue.
Async in slime means: same train.py, different rollout function, separate GPU pools. You trade a bounded amount of policy staleness for not waiting on the slowest trajectory.

blocks.prompt: A 64k-token response must wait while 32k tokens of other requests are decoded because its KV cache was evicted. Async rollout hides waiting between phases. Does it fix this case too?
blocks.reveal: Not by itself. The v0.1.0 blog counts this as 64k + 32k = 96k tokens of decode time, 1.5x the sample's own length, and the cause is KV cache overflow inside one engine, not the training barrier. The fixes it names are on the inference side: more KV cache (higher `mem_fraction` after offload), FP8 rollout, DeepEP (DeepSeek's library for the GPU-to-GPU traffic that sends tokens to their experts and back) and speculative decoding (a cheap draft proposes several tokens and the model checks them in one pass) to raise per-sample decode speed.

blocks.question: Rollout takes 300 s, training 300 s and sync 48 s per round on separate pools. Ignoring all overheads, what is the best case for fully async?
options: 348 s per round, about 1.86x faster than 648 s
648 s per round, the same as sync
300 s per round
48 s per round
blocks.explain: The bound is max(t_R, t_T) + t_W = 300 + 48 = 348 s against 300 + 300 + 48 = 648 s serial. Weight sync is not hidden in this model, so the round cannot drop to 300 s.

blocks.question: A teammate enables fully async rollout on a colocated 8-GPU job and sees no speedup. Why?
options: Fully async only works with PPO
The default --sglang-server-concurrency is too low
With colocation rollout and training share GPUs and must take turns, so there are no independent resources to overlap
Fully async requires delta weight sync
blocks.explain: The docs say fully async needs separate GPUs for meaningful overlap. On shared GPUs the phases still alternate, so the async bound does not apply.

lessons.title: Train-rollout mismatch in slime: TIS, IcePop, R3 and score centering

blocks.md:
One token, two numbers. SGLang sampled it and reported log probability -1.70; Megatron, recomputing the same token with the same weights, gets -0.31. Their ratio is $e^{-0.31-(-1.70)} = e^{1.39} = 4.0$: the trainer thinks this token is four times likelier than the engine that actually picked it.

Why two correct programs disagree (kernels, reduction order, FP8 rollout, MoE routing flips) and why sampling from one policy breaks the on-policy assumptions of another are taught in the RL post-training infrastructure course, lessons 7 and 8. This lesson is about the switches slime ships for the gap and what each one logs.

slime's [policy-mismatch guide](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/docs/en/advanced/policy-mismatch.md) names three policies, and each maps to a field you have already met:

- $q$: the behavior distribution that actually sampled the token, including quantization and possibly older weights. In slime, `rollout_log_probs` from SGLang's `output_token_logprobs` (lesson 5).
- $p_0$: the frozen trainer before the update, the old log probs Megatron recomputes (lesson 6).
- $p_\theta$: the trainable policy in the gradient pass.

PPO's ratio $r = p_\theta / p_0$ limits how far one update moves. A separate behavior ratio $\rho = p_0 / q$ corrects for who sampled. Before any clipping their product is $p_\theta / q$.

blocks.tex: \rho_t = e^{\log p_0(a_t) - \log q(a_t)},\qquad w_{\text{TIS}} = \operatorname{clip}(\rho_t, L, U),\qquad w_{\text{ice}} = \rho_t\,\mathbf{1}[L \le \rho_t \le U],\qquad \ell_t \leftarrow \operatorname{sg}(w)\,\ell_t
blocks.caption: The per-token behavior weight and slime's two built-in rules. sg is stop-gradient: the weight scales the token's PPO loss but is not itself differentiated.

blocks.md:
**TIS** (truncated importance sampling) is `--use-tis`. The built-in `vanilla_tis_function` computes $\rho$ from the old log probs and `rollout_log_probs`, clips it to [`--tis-clip-low`, `--tis-clip`] (defaults 0 and 2) and multiplies each token's loss by it. With `--pg-loss-type reinforce`, as in lesson 9's script, the numerator is the detached current policy instead of $p_0$. Capping weights limits outliers but is biased: the guide derives the bias as the mass above $U$ that is cut off, and notes that a per-token weight never corrects the distribution of the prefix that led to the token.

**IcePop**, from the Ling team's [Ring-1T report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18855), keeps $\rho$ inside the band and sets it to zero outside. slime ships it as a TIS callback: `--use-tis --custom-tis-function-path slime.backends.megatron_utils.loss.icepop_function --tis-clip-low 0.5 --tis-clip 2`. The callback zeroes weights but does not renormalize: masked tokens still count in the loss denominator.

blocks.prompt: Take the token above with rho = 4.0 and the guide's lab settings (TIS clipped to [0, 2], IcePop band [0.5, 2]). What weight does each rule give it?
blocks.reveal: TIS gives it 2: the weight is capped at U but the token still pushes, with half the correction it asked for. IcePop gives it 0: the token is treated as untrustworthy and contributes nothing. The guide calls these distinct estimators, not two settings of one.

blocks.title: Five tokens, three rules (computed with slime's importance_weights)

scenes.caption: p0 log probs -0.50, -1.00, -2.00, -0.31, -3.00; SGLang's q log probs -0.50, -1.20, -1.70, -1.70, -2.00. No correction: every token weighs 1, total 5.0.
TIS [0, 2]: only token 4 is cut, from 4.01 to 2.0. Total weight 5.33, tis_clipfrac 0.2. Token 5 keeps its small weight 0.37 because the lower bound is 0.
IcePop [0.5, 2]: tokens 4 and 5 fall outside the band and get weight 0. Total 2.96 from 3 surviving tokens, clipfrac 0.4, and the denominator still counts 5.

blocks.md:
What gets logged: `tis` (the mean $\rho$), `tis_clipfrac` (fraction of tokens whose weight differs from $\rho$), `tis_abs` (mean of $|\rho - 1|$), `ois` (the mean of $p_\theta / p_0$) and `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff`, the mean of $|\log p_0 - \log q|$, which is 0.578 for the five tokens above. IcePop reuses the same metric names.

Three related switches. `--get-mismatch-metrics` logs the gap without changing the loss; startup asserts that it comes with a `--custom-tis-function-path` such as the helper below. `--use-rollout-logprobs` bypasses the recompute and uses $q$ itself as the old policy. And [examples/train_infer_mismatch_helper](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/examples/train_infer_mismatch_helper/README.md) plugs in through `--custom-tis-function-path` with token, sequence or geometric-mean weights, truncate, mask or clip modes, rejection sampling, and a veto that drops a whole sequence if any token's ratio falls below a threshold such as 1e-4.

**R3** (rollout routing replay, [Ma et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370)) is `--use-rollout-routing-replay`. For an MoE model, slime-managed SGLang returns the experts it routed each token to; external engines must be launched with `--enable-return-routed-experts`. Samples carry them as `rollout_routed_experts`, one row per token position except the last, holding the top-k expert ids of every layer as int32 (the dtype slime decodes from SGLang), and the trainer forces those routes in its forward passes. That removes the expert-selection part of the gap, not the numerical part, and means nothing for a dense model.

Storage is concrete: Qwen3-30B-A3B routes 8 experts in each of 48 layers, so 384 int32 ids or 1,536 bytes per token, about 50.3 MB for a 32,768-token sample. Do not confuse it with `--use-routing-replay`, the GSPO paper's variant, which records routes during the trainer's own old-log-prob pass and replays them in the gradient pass without involving SGLang.

**Score centering** (`--use-score-centering`, [the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20807)) attacks a different symptom: under $q$ the expected score $\nabla \log p$ is no longer zero, so the baseline stops cancelling. slime stores the sampler's top 128 log probs per token (`--score-centering-top-k`), or the full top-p support, and adds a correction that re-centers the weighted score. It requires the REINFORCE objective (`--pg-loss-type reinforce`, no PPO clip, no GSPO or CISPO), positive temperature, `top_k -1`, `min_p 0`, no sampling penalties or constrained decoding, and an SGLang image built with slime's top-p patch. Lesson 9's example script turns it on together with TIS.

Determinism is related but not the same. `--sglang-enable-deterministic-inference` plus Megatron's `--deterministic-mode` make each side repeatable; making the two sides agree bit for bit is currently supported only for the GLM-5 structure with a patched stack.

A falling `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff` is not proof of better learning, and a rising `tis_clipfrac` is not fixed by widening the clip: under IcePop every clipped token is lost signal, and under TIS a wider band lets rare tokens dominate. The guide's protocol: hold data, seed and evaluation fixed, change one mechanism at a time, and read reward alongside the mismatch metrics and, when async, staleness.

slime treats SGLang as a behavior policy q. TIS caps the correction, IcePop drops out-of-band tokens, R3 removes MoE routing flips at the source, and score centering repairs the baseline. All need rollout log probs on every sample, and all are judged by the same few metrics.

blocks.question: An FP8-rollout run on an MoE model shows `tis_clipfrac` climbing from 0.002 to 0.1 over a few hundred rollouts while reward stalls. Following slime's guidance, which change comes first?
options: Raise --tis-clip to 20 so fewer tokens are clipped
Switch to --use-rollout-logprobs to skip the trainer recompute
Enable --use-rollout-routing-replay to remove routing flips at the source, keep TIS, and compare clipfrac and log-prob gap with that single change
Turn TIS off, since clipping shows it is not working
blocks.explain: On an MoE model a large share of the gap comes from expert selection, which R3 removes; it is independent of TIS. Widening the clip only lets outliers through, bypassing the recompute removes the correction (slime even refuses it with `--use-tis` under the PPO loss), and turning TIS off leaves the gap uncorrected. Change one mechanism at a time and watch the metrics.

blocks.question: You move an R3 run from slime-managed engines to an external SGLang deployment. Batch conversion now fails with "Rollout routed experts are missing for live sample indices". What fixes it?
options: Drop --use-tis
Launch the external engines with --enable-return-routed-experts so responses carry the routes
Set --rollout-top-p below 1
Convert the model to FP8
blocks.explain: slime-managed engines request routed experts automatically; external engines keep their own launch flags. BatchBuilder raises this error when R3 is on and live samples lack rollout_routed_experts.

lessons.title: Launching and debugging a slime run

blocks.md: The quick start uses a prebuilt Docker image (`slimerl/slime:latest` or `slimerl/slime:latest-cu130`, both CUDA 13.0 builds) that pins compatible SGLang, Megatron and patch versions; a conda script (`build_conda.sh`) exists for installs without Docker. The model needs two copies: a Hugging Face checkpoint for SGLang and a Megatron **torch_dist** checkpoint for training, because Megatron cannot read Hugging Face checkpoints directly. torch_dist is the recommended format since it re-shards automatically when parallelism changes.

blocks.code:
# on the host
docker pull slimerl/slime:latest-cu130
git clone https://github.com/THUDM/slime.git && cd slime
# inside the container: install your checkout, then fetch the model
pip install -e . --no-deps
hf download Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 --local-dir /root/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
# convert HF weights to Megatron torch_dist for --ref-load
source scripts/models/qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.sh
PYTHONPATH=/root/Megatron-LM python tools/convert_hf_to_torch_dist.py \
    ${MODEL_ARGS[@]} \
    --hf-checkpoint /root/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 \
    --save /root/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507_torch_dist
# start Ray and submit train.py (colocated, 8 GPUs)
bash scripts/run-qwen3-4B.sh
blocks.caption: Commands from the slime quick start and the search-r1 README; the example script expects the dapo-math-17k data (about 17,000 math problems with integer answers, released with DAPO) and the paths it names.

blocks.md: The script also uses two more Megatron parallelism flags. **Sequence parallelism** splits the activations of layers such as layer norm and dropout along the sequence across the tensor-parallel GPUs, so each GPU stores only its slice. **Context parallelism (CP)** splits each long sequence across GPUs, each holding a slice of the tokens and exchanging keys and values for attention. A **micro-batch** is the chunk of sequences processed in one forward and backward pass.

blocks.title: Reading scripts/run-qwen3-4B.sh (abridged)
blocks.code:
CKPT_ARGS:  --hf-checkpoint /root/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
            --ref-load /root/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507_torch_dist
            --load /root/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507_slime/
            --save /root/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507_slime/ --save-interval 20
ROLLOUT_ARGS: --prompt-data /root/dapo-math-17k/dapo-math-17k.jsonl
            --input-key prompt --label-key label --apply-chat-template
            --rm-type deepscaler
            --rollout-batch-size 32
            --n-samples-per-prompt 8
            --global-batch-size 256
EVAL_ARGS:  --eval-interval 20 --eval-prompt-data aime /root/aime-2024/aime-2024.jsonl
PERF_ARGS:  --tensor-model-parallel-size 2 --sequence-parallel
            --context-parallel-size 2
            --use-dynamic-batch-size --max-tokens-per-gpu 9216
GRPO_ARGS:  --advantage-estimator grpo --use-score-centering
            --pg-loss-type reinforce --use-tis --tis-clip-low 0 --tis-clip 2
            --disable-grpo-std-normalization --calculate-per-token-loss
            --use-kl-loss --kl-loss-coef 0.00 --kl-loss-type low_var_kl
SGLANG_ARGS: --rollout-num-gpus-per-engine 2
            --sglang-mem-fraction-static 0.7
ray job submit ... -- python3 train.py
            --actor-num-nodes 1 --actor-num-gpus-per-node $NUM_GPUS
            --colocate

scenes.caption: Checkpoints: SGLang starts from the HF checkpoint, the reference model loads the converted torch_dist copy, and the actor resumes from --load if it holds a checkpoint, else from --ref-load. A checkpoint is saved every 20 rollouts.
Each rollout takes 32 prompts from the prompt and label fields, rendered with the chat template, and samples 8 responses for each, scored by the deepscaler rule-based reward: 32 x 8 = 256 samples.
--global-batch-size counts samples, not prompts. 256 samples / 256 per step = 1 optimizer step per rollout, so this run is fully on-policy within a rollout.
Every 20 rollouts the policy is evaluated on AIME 2024 and logged under eval/aime (lesson 10).
Megatron parallelism passes straight through: TP 2 with sequence parallelism and CP 2. Dynamic batching packs sequences up to 9216 tokens per GPU instead of a fixed micro-batch.

The objective (lessons 6 and 8): group-centered rewards without std division, a REINFORCE loss with score centering and TIS, per-token reduction. --use-kl-loss with coefficient 0 adds no penalty but loads the reference model, so its KL is still logged.
SGLang runs 2-GPU engines with 70 percent static memory; with --colocate on 8 GPUs that means 4 engines that share GPUs with the Megatron actor.

blocks.title: Optimizer steps per rollout (32 prompts x 8 samples)

scenes.caption: steps = rollout_batch_size x n_samples_per_prompt / global_batch_size. The example script uses 256, one step per rollout.
Halving the global batch doubles the steps. Later steps in the same rollout train on data from an older policy, which is mildly off-policy. --num-steps-per-rollout sets this directly.

blocks.md: Two practical details from the usage guide. First, slime trains on packed variable-length sequences, so you do not set `--seq-length`. Second, the model shape flags (`--num-layers`, `--hidden-size` and so on) come from a model file in `scripts/models/`, which is why the script sources a model file before building its argument arrays.

Because rollout and training are separate engines, slime lets you debug them separately:

- `--debug-rollout-only`: does not load Megatron; only SGLang starts. Use it to tune inference or check that a checkpoint generates sensible text.
- `--debug-train-only`: does not load SGLang; only Megatron starts.
- `--save-debug-rollout-data` then `--load-debug-rollout-data`: freeze one rollout to disk and replay it into training, for example while trying different parallelism settings.

The v0.1.0 blog also lists two CI invariants worth checking in your own runs: on the first rollout the recomputed log probs must exactly equal the reference model's, and the `ppo_kl` of the first training step within each rollout must be exactly 0. `ppo_kl` is the mean over tokens of the old log prob minus the new one, an estimate of the KL (Kullback-Leibler) divergence, a measure of how far one probability distribution is from another that is 0 only when they match. That divergence, from the old policy to the new one, is the average of log old minus log new over tokens drawn from the old policy; the rollout tokens were drawn from that policy (up to lesson 8's engine mismatch), so the plain mean of the difference estimates it. Both invariants follow from the setup: the actor starts from the reference model's weights, and the first step of each rollout trains on data from exactly the current weights, so any non-zero gap points to a bug.

Both invariants need pieces from lesson 6: a reference model, which slime loads only with `--use-kl-loss` or a non-zero `--kl-coef`, and the old log probs recomputed on the actor. Today's CI asserts first-step `ppo_kl` below 1e-8 and, on the very first step, the reference KL loss below 1e-8, skipping the latter with R3 or top-p replay, where the actor and reference legitimately see different routes or supports.

To move this example to separate pools, drop `--colocate` and set `--rollout-num-gpus` (plus actor nodes and GPUs) so the two pools add up to your cluster. To go agentic, add `--custom-generate-function-path` and `--custom-rm-path`; to go fully async, set `--rollout-function-path` to the fully async rollout. Lesson 10 covers how to tell whether the run is working.

blocks.question: The actor's `--load` directory is empty on the first launch. What does the actor initialize from?
options: Random weights
The `--hf-checkpoint`, converted on the fly
The `--ref-load` torch_dist checkpoint
It refuses to start
blocks.explain: The usage guide: if `--load` is unset, missing, or lacks `latest_checkpointed_iteration.txt`, the actor is initialized from the `--ref-load` checkpoint. The HF checkpoint only initializes SGLang.

blocks.question: Generations look like garbage, and you suspect either the FP8 rollout checkpoint or the weight sync. Which first step isolates the inference side cheaply?
options: Run with `--debug-train-only`
Run with `--debug-rollout-only` on a few GPUs to see whether SGLang alone generates coherent text from the checkpoint
Increase `--global-batch-size`
Disable `--colocate`
blocks.explain: The debug guide suggests `--debug-rollout-only` with few GPUs to test the quantized checkpoint alone; if it is fine, look at the sync with `--check-weight-update-equal`.

lessons.title: Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery

blocks.md:
A run that launches is not a run that works. slime's [experiment guide](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/docs/en/get_started/experiment-guide.md) gives an order for deciding:

1. Read generated responses first.
2. Check reward and the reference and trainer log probs.
3. Then inspect train-rollout mismatch and correction clipping or masking.
4. With fully async rollout, inspect staleness.

"A fast run with meaningless rewards is not progress." This lesson covers the tools for each step and what to do when a long run dies.

Metrics go to W&B with `--use-wandb` or TensorBoard with `--use-tensorboard`. Four families matter: `rollout/` (per-rollout means such as `raw_reward`, `response_lengths`, `log_probs`, `ref_log_probs`, and dynamic-sampling drop ratios), `train/` (`loss`, `pg_loss`, `pg_clipfrac`, `ppo_kl`, `kl_loss`, `entropy_loss`, `grad_norm`, and when on, `tis_clipfrac` and `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff`), `eval/` per held-out dataset, and `perf/` timings (`perf/step_time`, `perf/actor_train_time`, and SGLang request latencies aggregated once per rollout). Fully async runs add `staleness/mean` and `staleness/max`.

To read responses, dump rollouts with `--save-debug-rollout-data /path/rollout_{rollout_id}.pt`; `tools/trace_timeline_viewer.py` renders the per-request timing in those dumps.

blocks.title: Four illustrative runs, logged every 20 rollouts

scenes.caption: Columns are rollouts 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100. A healthy run (invented numbers for practice, not a measurement): reward and eval rise together, length grows slowly, first-step ppo_kl is exactly 0, mismatch clipping stays tiny.
Run B: everything looks fine except first-step ppo_kl, which should be 0 by construction (lesson 6). Something makes the same weights give different log probs.
Run C: reward stays near zero while responses keep getting longer and eval falls. The numbers say something is wrong; only the responses say what.
Run D: --hf-checkpoint switched to an FP8 checkpoint at rollout 60. tis_clipfrac jumps from 0.001 to 0.09 and keeps rising while reward and eval flatten.

blocks.md:
Diagnosing them with the [debug guide](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/docs/en/developer_guide/debug.md):

- **Run B.** First-step KL can be non-zero only when p0 comes from a separate pass (lesson 6); then the guide points to non-deterministic kernels, for example Transformer Engine's fused attention under CP (fixed with `--attention-backend flash`) or MoE without `--moe-permute-fusion`. Check that log probs and reference log probs were exactly equal on the first rollout.
- **Run C.** Read responses before touching the algorithm. With almost every group scoring all zeros, those groups carry zero advantage (or are dropped by dynamic sampling) and a few mixed groups steer training. Common causes: an answer format the reward never parses, the wrong `--label-key`, a missing `--apply-chat-template`, or responses cut off at the length limit before they answer.
- **Run D.** The FP8 switch widened the gap between q and p0. Check the checkpoint's `quantization_config` and `--check-weight-update-equal` (lesson 4), then apply lesson 8's corrections one at a time.

Held-out evaluation is built into the synchronous loop. The example script uses:

`--eval-interval 20 --eval-prompt-data aime /root/aime-2024/aime-2024.jsonl --n-samples-per-eval-prompt 16`

`--eval-prompt-data` takes name and path pairs, so several datasets log separately under `eval/`; `--eval-config` takes a YAML file instead. Evaluation has its own sampling flags (`--eval-temperature`, `--eval-top-p`, `--eval-max-response-len`). train.py evaluates once before rollout 0 (not on a resume) unless `--skip-eval-before-train`, then after the weight update of every rollout whose number plus one is a multiple of the interval, and at epoch boundaries. The fully async rollout implements no evaluation, so async runs need a separate evaluation job.

Serving-side metrics are different. slime stores no per-second Prometheus data: SGLang and the router only expose `/metrics` and `/engine_metrics`, so for queue lengths and latency histograms over time you run Prometheus next to the job, scraping the router, with `--storage.tsdb.path` on persistent storage ([observability guide](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/docs/en/advanced/observability.md)).

**Checkpoints.** `--save DIR --save-interval N` saves after rollout `r` whenever $(r+1)$ is a multiple of N, and also after the last rollout and at epoch boundaries. `--load DIR` resumes from the latest checkpoint there at rollout saved + 1 (lesson 9: if `--load` is empty, the actor starts from `--ref-load`). Recovery needs torch_dist checkpoints with RNG and optimizer state; `--no-save-optim` makes checkpoints smaller but disables resumption unless the optimizer is stateless.

**Retaining recovery data.** The [fault-tolerance guide](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/docs/en/advanced/fault-tolerance.md) asks for one of two things from the first launch: straw transport (`--rollout-data-transport straw --rollout-data-dir ...`, lesson 7) or `--save-debug-rollout-data` with `{rollout_id}` in the path. Either keeps the generated samples, tokens and reward results of every batch after the last checkpoint.

blocks.title: Resubmitting after a Megatron failure (save interval 50)

scenes.caption: Rollout 299 finishes: (299 + 1) is a multiple of 50, so the model, optimizer, scheduler and RNG state are saved. Every later batch is persisted by straw as it is built.
Training on rollout 340 runs out of GPU memory. The driver and trainers exit, but the Ray cluster, SGLang engines and routers stay up.

You change TP, CP, micro-batch or the token budget and resubmit train.py to the same Ray cluster. It finds ServingCluster, the named, detached Ray actor that owns routers and engines and outlives the job, by session identity.

New trainers load checkpoint 299 with RNG and optimizer state. Retained batches from 300 on are repartitioned for the new layout and retrained, without regenerating samples or rerunning reward postprocessing.
Training catches up, weights are pushed to the retained engines (serving weight versions keep increasing across restarts), and new rollouts continue.

blocks.md:
Rules for that resubmission: keep the model, rollout configuration, global batch size and session identity; do not stop Ray, recreate the serving container or run `pkill sglang` between attempts. That matters because example scripts such as run-qwen3-4B.sh begin with exactly those cleanup commands, so skip them when restarting. The session identity is `--rollout-session-id` if set, otherwise derived from the straw directory and run id, the debug-data path, the `--save` path, or the model and rollout configuration, in that order.

Engines are watched too: slime polls SGLang's `/health_generate` (interval, first wait and timeout default to 600 s each, plus a check whenever a rollout finishes), removes failed engines from the router and restarts them before the next weight update.

Recovery has limits. Without straw or rollout dumps you keep the engines but cannot replay batches after the last checkpoint. If the ServingCluster actor or the whole Ray cluster is lost, you start serving again and resume from the checkpoint; node loss and preemption need your scheduler's help. A resume with a different TP or PP layout reinitializes RNG, so it is not bitwise identical.

Judge a run in order: responses, reward and log probs, mismatch, staleness, with a held-out eval from the start. Save on an interval you can afford to lose, keep straw or rollout dumps for the batches in between, and resubmit failed training to the same Ray cluster instead of tearing it down.

blocks.question: A run with `--save-interval 50`, straw transport and no epoch boundary nearby dies while training rollout 340. You resubmit to the same Ray cluster. Where does training resume, and what is lost?
options: From the checkpoint saved after rollout 299; the batches from 300 on are retrained from retained straw data, so no generated samples are lost
From rollout 340, because the engines kept their weights
From the checkpoint after rollout 300; batch 340 is regenerated
From the beginning, because the optimizer state is not saved
blocks.explain: Saves happen after rollout r when r + 1 is a multiple of 50, so the last one followed rollout 299. The new trainer loads it and retrains every batch after it, including batches that finished training but were never saved. straw kept their samples and rewards; only the training compute since the checkpoint is repeated.

blocks.question: A fully async agentic run sets `--eval-interval 20` and an AIME eval set, but no eval/ metrics ever appear. Why, and what should you do?
options: Eval runs only every 20 epochs
The eval set must be Parquet
--n-samples-per-eval-prompt defaults to 0
The fully async rollout implements no evaluation, so evaluate saved checkpoints in a separate job
blocks.explain: The experiment guide and the fully async README both say the continuous queue does not implement evaluation, which would conflict with the continuously running model. Evaluate saved checkpoints separately. --n-samples-per-eval-prompt defaults to 1.
